home.h1: What does good learning look like today?
home.intro: {n} ready-to-run activities built on the TCEA Essential Learning Expectations: {pl} for professional learning and {st} for K–16 classrooms. Each one weaves in Gen AI literacy, digital citizenship, or media literacy. Every activity comes with print-ready handouts, and {un} need no devices at all.

fw.title: The ELEs
fw.desc: Browse all 75 TCEA Essential Learning Expectation indicators and the activities that build each one.
fw.lede: TCEA's ELEs give teachers, students, coaches, school leaders, and anyone working with AI a common language for better learning. Each role has five key areas with three indicators each, written as “I know,” “I can,” and “I am aware.” Below each indicator are the activities in this bank that build it.
fw.source: Framework text from the TCEA Essential Learning Expectations (ELEs), CC-BY-SA 2024, tinyurl.com/tceaeles1. Alignment examples and TEKS/TEA correlations are quoted from the ELE documents.
g.title: Facilitator guide
g.desc: How to plan with the ELE Activity Bank: evidence first, a five-part planning check, and safe AI use.
g.lede: How the bank is built, and how to plan a session or lesson with it.
g.s1.h: Start with the evidence, not the tool
g.s1.p1: The updated ELEs ask one question of every lesson, workshop, tool pilot, and campus initiative: *what does good learning look like today?* Technology use by itself is not evidence of learning. So every activity here starts from what learners should produce: a claim with evidence, a verification move, a revised draft, a decision they can defend. Tools come second.
g.s1.p2: That is why every activity page has an **Evidence of learning** section, and a note answering **does it need a screen?** With growing pressure to limit screen time, an unplugged path is a feature, not a fallback.
g.s2.h: A planning check for any role
g.s2.p: Pick one lesson, PD session, tool pilot, or campus initiative. Choose the role lane that matters most, then ask what evidence is missing. If the work is strong, you can answer all five:
g.s2.teacher: **Teacher:** what is the teacher designing, and what evidence do they want?
g.s2.student: **Student:** what are learners doing, deciding, and explaining?
g.s2.coach: **Coach:** how will support happen? Listen, co-plan, model, measure, adjust.
g.s2.leader: **Leader:** what will leaders monitor? What is the vision, what evidence will guide us, what changes in instruction, who might be left out, and how will families understand the change?
g.s2.ai: **AI:** where does AI belong, if it belongs at all?
g.s4.h: How each activity is laid out
g.s4.glance: **At a glance:** time, mode, audience, group size, strands, and the ELE indicators it builds, each linked to the framework.
g.s4.steps: **Step by step:** a timed sequence with what to say and do, plus facilitator notes on likely misconceptions.
g.s4.paths: **Paper or screen:** how to run it with no devices, how to run it digitally, and whether the screen adds anything.
g.s4.evidence: **Evidence of learning:** what you should be able to see or collect if it worked.
g.s4.adapt: **Adaptations:** other grade bands, higher education, emergent bilingual learners, and more.
g.s4.handouts: **Handouts:** a print-ready packet on US Letter (cards, sorts, worksheets, organizers, readings, rubrics) with a facilitator key on the last page.
g.s5.h: Professional learning that models the classroom
g.s5.p: Most PL activities ask educators to do the task as learners first, then step back and debrief as teachers, coaches, or leaders. That double pass matters: people teach the version of a skill they have felt. Close every session with the “Take it to your students” step, and bring student evidence back to a PLC or coaching conversation.
g.s6.h: Using AI tools safely with students
g.s6.a: Use only tools your district or institution has approved, and follow their age requirements.
g.s6.b: With students under 13, the teacher drives any AI tool on a shared screen. Printed mock AI outputs work just as well for most lessons here.
g.s6.c: Never enter student names, grades, or other personal information into an AI tool.
g.s6.d: Every mock article, post, and AI output in these handouts is fictional, and labeled that way.
g.s7.p: Everything here is CC BY-SA 4.0. Copy it, translate it, and remix it for your campus with credit. To align your own lessons or PD to the ELEs, try the {assistant} or get the {pdf}.

std.title: Standards alignment
std.desc: How the ELE Activity Bank connects to the TEKS, the ELPS, Universal Design for Learning, and the Texas Student Success Tool.
std.lede: Every activity is built on the TCEA ELEs first. This page shows how the same activities also connect to the Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS), the English Language Proficiency Standards (ELPS), CAST's Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Guidelines 3.0, and the skills the Texas Student Success Tool (SST) will measure.
std.disclaimer: Standards are paraphrased and cited by section number, never quoted. Alignments are a good-faith planning aid, not an official correlation. Confirm current requirements at tea.texas.gov before adoption.
std.sst.p1: Under House Bill 8, the Student Success Tool replaces STAAR beginning in the 2027–28 school year. STAAR stays in place for 2026–27. Grades 3–8 will take beginning-of-year, middle-of-year, and end-of-year assessments; the Algebra I, Biology, English I, and U.S. History end-of-course exams keep an end-of-year test, with optional beginning- and middle-of-year checkpoints.
std.sst.p2: None of these activities is test prep, and none should become it. They build what the SST blueprints reward over time: reading closely and citing evidence, writing and revising a constructed response, analyzing sources and competing claims, and explaining a conclusion from data. TEA's own caution applies here too: every student expectation must still be taught in full, not just the ones a blueprint lists.
std.sst.p3: Use the three checkpoints as one teaching loop: set a baseline at the beginning of the year, regroup and reteach at the middle, and review growth at the end. The activities marked below give students regular, low-stakes practice with the reasoning those checkpoints look for.
std.sst.hub: SST Activities in the Learning Activities Hub
std.teks.p1: The Technology Applications TEKS (adopted 2022, required in grades K–8) include a digital citizenship strand with three substrands: social interactions (c)(8), ethics and laws (c)(9), and privacy, safety, and security (c)(10). They appear in §126.5–§126.10 for kindergarten through grade 5 and §126.17–§126.19 for grades 6–8. Gen AI activities also connect to the computational thinking, creativity and innovation, data literacy, and practical technology concepts strands.
std.teks.p2: Media literacy lives just as much in the English Language Arts and Reading TEKS: comprehension, response skills, multiple genres (including multimodal and digital texts), author's purpose and craft, composition, and inquiry and research. These are §110.2–§110.7 for K–5, §110.22–§110.24 for grades 6–8, and §110.36–§110.39 for English I–IV. Some activities also build the social studies skills strand and the science and engineering practices.
std.teks.p3: For professional learning activities, the TEKS listed are the student standards the educator is preparing to teach. Leadership and coaching sessions that don't lead straight to a student lesson list none, and neither do activities only for higher education.
std.elps.p1: The ELPS (19 TAC §74.4) apply in every content area. Their cross-curricular student expectations cover learning strategies, listening, speaking, reading, and writing, and instruction must be communicated, sequenced, and scaffolded to each student's English proficiency level: beginning, intermediate, advanced, or advanced high.
std.elps.p2: These activities give emergent bilingual students a lot to hold on to: cards that break ideas into small pieces, sorting that lets students show understanding before they can explain it, roles in discussion, and paper handouts with numbered paragraphs and drawing boxes. The whole site, including every handout, is also being translated into Spanish and Vietnamese, so students and families can work in their home language beside English.
std.elps.tips: Supports that work across the bank
std.elps.t1: **Cards and sorts:** read each card aloud once, point out cognates, and accept pointing or placing a card as a first answer before asking for a sentence.
std.elps.t2: **Readings and mock posts:** preview three to five key words with a picture or gesture, and use the paragraph numbers so students can cite evidence by number.
std.elps.t3: **Discussion:** give sentence stems ("I think this is ___ because ___"), assign roles, and let partners rehearse in any language before sharing in English.
std.elps.t4: **Worksheets:** allow drawing boxes, labeled sketches, and short phrases at beginning and intermediate levels; expect full sentences at advanced and advanced high.
std.elps.t5: **Home language:** hand out the Spanish or Vietnamese version of a packet alongside the English one.
std.udl.p1: CAST's UDL Guidelines 3.0 organize design around three principles: multiple means of engagement (the why of learning), representation (the what), and action and expression (the how). The goal is learner agency.
std.udl.p2: Several choices in this bank are UDL moves by design: every activity has an unplugged path and a digital path, handouts come in several formats, each activity lists adaptations for other grade bands and learners, and evidence of learning is named up front so goals are clear. The checkpoints below show where each activity goes further.

g.s8.h: Screen time: purpose, not just minutes
g.s8.p1: In Texas, the rules on phones changed first. HB 1481 (2025) requires every district and charter school to prohibit students from using personal communication devices during the school day, but the law explicitly excludes devices the school provides. How students use school-issued laptops and tablets is still each district's decision, and that is where the conversation has moved.
g.s8.p2: The research points the same way. The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2026 policy statement moves beyond simple time limits toward quality, context, and conversation. The Common Sense Census (2021) found that tweens average 5 hours 33 minutes and teens 8 hours 39 minutes of entertainment screen media a day, not counting school or homework, and only 8 and 14 minutes of that is spent creating. At school, the question isn't only how long, but for what: creating, researching, and practicing with feedback are not the same as watching.
g.s8.p3: This bank is built for that question. Every activity has an unplugged path and a plain answer to *does it need a screen?*, and {n} need no devices at all. There is no independent national measure of how much time students spend on school-issued devices, so start with your own data.
g.s8.src2: American Academy of Pediatrics, Digital Ecosystems, Children, and Adolescents (policy statement, Pediatrics, 2026)
g.s8.src4: The Common Sense Census: Media Use by Tweens and Teens, 2021
